body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Structured follow-up recommendation codes in radiology reports and completion of recommended imaging: a before-after study","authors":"Haddad-Lindqvist S, Okonkwo-Pierce M, Tanaka-Brandt L","year":2018,"venue":"Brightwater Journal of Radiology Practice","doi":"10.5555/bjrp.2018.0231","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"After our department introduced standard codes for follow-up recommendations in radiology reports, we compared 1,200 reports with an incidental finding before the change with 1,200 reports after it. Recommendations became more specific: the share naming a modality and an interval rose from 46 percent to 88 percent. Completion of recommended imaging within the stated interval rose from 51 percent to 58 percent. Completion was lowest for findings reported on emergency department examinations. The codes did not by themselves notify anyone, and completion was measured only within our own health system, so imaging done elsewhere was missed."},{"title":"A nurse navigator for incidental pulmonary nodules: follow-up completion over three years","authors":"Mwangi-Holt D, Castellanos-Achebe R","year":2020,"venue":"Thoracic Imaging Service Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A nurse navigator reviewed every chest CT report with an incidental pulmonary nodule and a follow-up recommendation, contacted the ordering clinician and, when needed, the patient, and booked the follow-up scan. Over three years, 2,406 patients were tracked. Follow-up completion within the recommended window was 79 percent, compared with 43 percent in the year before the navigator started. Completion was 64 percent among patients without a regular primary care clinician. The navigator post required one full-time position for about 800 new nodules a year. The comparison was with a single earlier year and did not adjust for changes in referral patterns."},{"title":"Automated alerts to ordering clinicians for actionable incidental findings: a controlled comparison across two hospitals","authors":"Lorenz-Adeyemi K, Whitcombe-Nakashima P, Oduya-Grant F","year":2022,"venue":"Clinical Informatics in Imaging","doi":"10.5555/cii.2022.0418","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One hospital sent an automated electronic health record alert to the ordering clinician for every report with an actionable incidental finding, while a sister hospital did not. Among 3,150 findings, follow-up was completed within the recommended interval for 62 percent at the alert hospital and 55 percent at the comparison hospital. Alerts were acknowledged within seven days for 71 percent of findings. When the ordering clinician was an emergency physician or a resident who had since rotated, acknowledgement fell to 38 percent. The hospitals differed in patient mix and in access to primary care."},{"title":"Letters sent directly to patients about incidental imaging findings: effect on follow-up and on patient worry","authors":"Brennan-Obi C, Varga-Moreau A","year":2016,"venue":"Patient Communication in Imaging","doi":"10.5555/pci.2016.0067","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Patients with an incidental finding that needed follow-up imaging were sent a plain-language letter by the radiology department in addition to the usual report to their clinician. Compared with a matched group from the previous year, follow-up completion rose from 48 percent to 60 percent. In a questionnaire returned by 212 of 390 patients who received letters, 17 percent said the letter made them very worried, and most said they would have preferred to hear about the finding from their own clinician. Letters were sent only in English, and patients without a fixed address were not reached."},{"title":"Why follow-up of incidental imaging findings fails: a structured review of reported failure points","authors":"Petit-Ramirez J, Soto-Lindgren E, Adu-Hargreave N","year":2024,"venue":"Health Systems Safety Review","doi":"10.5555/hssr.2024.0102","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 37 published reports of follow-up failures for incidental imaging findings and classified where the loop broke. The most frequent failure points were a recommendation that did not reach a clinician who took responsibility, vague recommendations without a modality or interval, patients seen only in emergency or inpatient settings without a follow-up clinician, and loss of contact after patients moved. Few reports described failures among patients who did not speak the local language. Most reports came from single academic centres, and the review did not assess the quality of the included reports."},{"title":"Follow-up completion for incidental adrenal and renal lesions among patients without a primary care clinician","authors":"Rasmussen-Diallo T, Kimura-Fenwick O","year":2021,"venue":"Urban Health Imaging","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Among 1,038 patients with an incidental adrenal or renal lesion that needed follow-up imaging, 612 had a primary care clinician on record. Follow-up completion within one year was 67 percent for patients with a primary care clinician and 34 percent for those without. Patients first imaged in the emergency department made up most of those without a clinician. Completion was also lower among patients living in the most deprived neighbourhoods. The study used one health system's records and could not capture imaging done elsewhere, so completion may be underestimated for patients who moved."},{"title":"Combining report codes, a tracking list and navigators for incidental findings: five years at a regional health system","authors":"Quist-Ferreira H, Nwosu-Blake G, Holm-Achterberg I","year":2025,"venue":"Brightwater Journal of Radiology Practice","doi":"10.5555/bjrp.2025.0011","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A regional health system combined structured recommendation codes, a tracking list of every open recommendation, and two navigators who closed the loop with clinicians and patients. Over five years, 14,820 recommendations were tracked. Completion within the recommended interval rose from 49 percent in the first year to 76 percent in the fifth year. The programme needed 2.5 full-time staff, mostly navigator time and list maintenance. The system was introduced in stages alongside other safety work, so the contribution of each component cannot be separated, and there was no comparison health system."}]}
